result: SARS-CoV-2 exhibits exponential growth dynamics with R0≈2-4, leading to case doubling every ~3 days and 1000-fold growth in approximately one month without countermeasures.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 present a mathematically consistent model of viral spread based on established R0 values (C1) and generation time (C2-C3). The calculations for doubling time (C4-C5) and exponential growth projections (C6-C7) follow logically from these parameters and are supported by cited epidemiological studies (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).

result: An effective reproduction number (Re) below 1 will cause SARS-CoV-2 infections to decline.
evaluation: Claim C8 represents fundamental epidemiological knowledge that is well-established and mathematically sound. When each infection generates fewer than one new infection on average, the epidemic necessarily declines.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 incubation period has a median of approximately 5 days, with 97.5% of symptomatic cases developing symptoms within 11.5 days and approximately 99% within 14 days.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C117-C120 are well-supported by multiple peer-reviewed epidemiological studies (Lauer et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020b) with consistent estimates across different datasets. The 14-day quarantine period (C10) is justified by the incubation period distribution.

result: N95 masks can filter SARS-CoV-2 virions and respiratory droplets, providing protection against both surface and airborne transmission.
evaluation: Claims C11-C16 are supported by established mask specifications (C11), empirical filtration data (C12), viral size measurements (C13), and respiratory droplet characterization (C14-C15). The inference about protection (C16) is reasonable given the filtration efficiency exceeds viral and droplet sizes, though the manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about dominant transmission modes.

result: SARS-CoV-2 is a beta-coronavirus with a ~30 kb RNA genome, distinct from influenza viruses but similar in genome structure to common cold coronaviruses while differing in sequence identity (~50%) and disease severity.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are supported by genomic data and established virological knowledge. The comparisons to influenza (C18-C19) and cold-causing coronaviruses (C20-C23) are based on genomic analyses presented in the manuscript and are consistent with known viral taxonomy.

result: Coronaviruses have the largest RNA viral genomes (~30 kb) and possess a proofreading exonuclease (ExoN) that results in lower mutation rates (~10⁻⁶ per site per cycle) compared to influenza (~3×10⁻⁵).
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by established virological knowledge (C24-C25) and peer-reviewed mutation rate measurements (C26, Sanjuán et al., 2010). The mechanistic link between proofreading and low mutation rate is well-established in coronavirus biology.

result: SARS-CoV-2 has 10 genes producing 26 proteins, including a polyprotein (orf1ab) cleaved into 16 proteins, with clear biochemical functions assigned to only about half of the gene products.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by NCBI genomic annotations and established coronavirus biology. Claim C29 represents an honest assessment of current knowledge limitations, which is appropriate for a review article.

result: The evolutionary rate of SARS-CoV-2 (~10⁻³ mutations/site/year) is consistent with the mutation rate (~10⁻⁶ per cycle) multiplied by replication cycles per year (~10³), indicating near-continuous replication in the wild.
evaluation: Claims C30-C36 present a coherent quantitative framework linking mutation rate, replication kinetics, and evolutionary rate. The calculation (C32-C34) is mathematically sound, and the inference about continuous replication (C35) is reasonable given the consistency between predicted and observed rates. Claim C36 provides a useful quantitative insight about mutational diversity in clinical samples.

result: SARS-CoV-2 RNA persists on surfaces longer than infectious virions, with stability varying by surface type, temperature, and humidity.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are supported by multiple peer-reviewed studies (Woelfel et al., 2020; Moriarty et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2020). The distinction between RNA detection and infectivity (C37, C39) is an important methodological point well-supported by the cited literature.

result: R0 estimates the average number of new infections from a single case in a fully susceptible population without countermeasures, and varies by locale due to cultural and geographic factors.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 provide standard epidemiological definitions that are well-established in the field. These are foundational concepts necessary for interpreting the quantitative results presented elsewhere in the manuscript.

result: Viral RNA is detectable for >1 week in moderate cases and >2 weeks in severe cases, though direct measurement of latent and infectious periods at the individual level is extremely challenging.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by ECDC data, while C49 provides important context about measurement challenges. This appropriately acknowledges limitations in epidemiological parameter estimation.

result: RT-qPCR measures viral RNA copies but not necessarily infectious virions, while TCID50 measures infectivity and typically yields lower counts than RT-qPCR, though even small doses (~0.1 TCID50) can cause infection.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 accurately describe established virological methods and their limitations. The comparison between RT-qPCR and TCID50 (C53) is supported by cited studies, and the infectivity data for common cold (C54) provides useful context, though direct SARS-CoV-2 data would strengthen this result.

result: The case fatality rate (CFR) varies from 1-15% across countries and tends to overestimate the true infection fatality rate (IFR) due to underascertainment of mild and asymptomatic cases.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59 provide standard epidemiological definitions and acknowledge important biases in CFR estimation. The variation in CFR (C56) is supported by epidemiological data, and the distinction between CFR and IFR (C58-C59) is conceptually sound and important for interpreting mortality statistics.

result: SARS-CoV-2 releases progeny by continuous budding rather than cell lysis, with the eclipse period measuring time to intracellular virion appearance and the latent period measuring time to extracellular virus release.
evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by Park et al., 2020b, while C61-C62 provide standard virological definitions. These concepts are important for understanding viral replication kinetics.

result: Unlike seasonal flu, SARS-CoV-2 transmission commonly occurs pre-symptomatically, with peak infectiousness beginning ~2 days before symptom onset and diagnosis typically occurring after peak infectiousness has passed.
evaluation: Claims C63-C70 are well-supported by multiple peer-reviewed studies (Ip et al., 2017; Ferretti et al., 2020; He et al., 2020). The contrast with influenza (C63-C64) and the timing of peak infectiousness relative to symptoms (C65-C66) and diagnosis (C68-C69) represent critical findings for public health interventions.

result: A large fraction of SARS-CoV-2 cases are asymptomatic (>50% in children and young adults), with modeling studies assuming asymptomatic infections are 10-80% as contagious as symptomatic ones.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by epidemiological observations, and C72 is supported by Davies et al., 2020. However, the wide range in C73 (10-80%) reflects substantial uncertainty about asymptomatic transmission, which the manuscript appropriately acknowledges as a "crucial gap in our understanding." This uncertainty limits confidence in epidemic projections.

result: SARS-CoV-2 virions are generally spherical with diameters of 60-140 nm, containing ~90 spike trimers of 9-12 nm length.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by electron microscopy data (Zhu et al., 2020) and structural modeling (Neuman et al., 2011). These structural parameters are important for understanding viral entry and immune recognition.

result: Receptor binding affinity (Kd) measurements for SARS-CoV-2 spike/RBD to ACE2 range from ~1-40 nM across different studies, with the main disagreement in dissociation rate constants (koff).
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 report binding affinity data from multiple peer-reviewed studies using different methods (biolayer interferometry, surface plasmon resonance). The variation in reported values (C83) is appropriately acknowledged, and the identification of koff as the main source of disagreement is a useful observation, though the biological significance of this variation could be better addressed.

result: Coronavirus virions contain approximately 1100 membrane protein dimers, 15-30 envelope proteins, and 730-2200 nucleoproteins.
evaluation: Claims C84 and C86 are supported by Neuman et al., 2011, while C85 is from a TGEV coronavirus study (Godet et al., 1992). The use of data from related coronaviruses is reasonable given structural conservation, though SARS-CoV-2-specific measurements would be preferable.

result: SARS-CoV-2 has a ~30 kb single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome with 10 open reading frames, which is typical for coronaviruses.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by NCBI genomic data and peer-reviewed genomic analyses (Wu et al., 2020b; Smith and Denison, 2012). These are well-established genomic characteristics.

result: Evolutionary rates for SARS, MERS, and OC43 range from 0.27-2.38×10⁻³ substitutions/site/year, with a measured mutation rate of 3.5×10⁻⁶ per site per cycle for murine hepatitis virus.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by peer-reviewed studies (Koyama et al., 2020; Sanjuán et al., 2010). These provide important context for understanding SARS-CoV-2 evolution, though the manuscript appropriately notes that C91 is from a related coronavirus.

result: SARS-CoV-2 shows varying degrees of genomic similarity to related viruses: 96% to bat coronavirus RaTG13, 91% to pangolin CoV, 80% to SARS-CoV-1, and 50-55% to common cold coronaviruses and MERS.
evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by genomic sequence alignments from NCBI and peer-reviewed studies (Zhang et al., 2020). These phylogenetic relationships are important for understanding viral origins and evolution.

result: SARS-CoV-1 is internalized within 10-15 minutes, with a complete replication cycle taking 7-8 hours from adsorption to progeny release.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by peer-reviewed studies on SARS-CoV-1 (Schneider et al., 2012; Ng et al., 2003). While these are SARS-CoV-1 data rather than SARS-CoV-2, the manuscript appropriately indicates this, and the values likely provide reasonable estimates given viral similarity.

result: The burst size for MHV coronavirus is approximately 600-700 plaque-forming units per cell.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by Hirano et al., 1976, though this is MHV data rather than SARS-CoV-2. The manuscript appropriately notes that "more research is needed to verify these values for SARS-CoV-2."

result: SARS-CoV-2 infects type I and II pneumocytes, alveolar macrophages, and mucous gland epithelial cells via ACE2 receptor binding.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by histopathology studies (Shieh et al., 2005), molecular biology studies (Walls et al., 2020), and animal model data (Rockx et al., 2020). The identification of target cell types is important for understanding disease pathogenesis.

result: Type II pneumocytes have a mean volume of ~763 μm³, while alveolar macrophages are larger at ~2,491 μm³.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by morphometry studies (Fehrenbach et al., 1995; Crapo et al., 1982). These cellular parameters provide context for understanding viral replication capacity.

result: SARS-CoV-2 antibody seroconversion occurs with median times of 11-14 days for different antibody types, with high seropositivity rates (88-100%) by day 14 after symptom onset.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by serological studies (Zhao et al., 2020; To et al., 2020). These data are important for understanding immune response kinetics and interpreting serological tests.

result: SARS-specific antibodies were maintained for an average of 2 years in SARS patients, with significant reduction in the third year.
evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by Wu et al., 2007 longitudinal study of SARS-CoV-1 patients. While this is SARS-CoV-1 data, it provides relevant context for understanding potential antibody durability for SARS-CoV-2.

result: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected on Diamond Princess cabin surfaces up to 17 days after vacating but before disinfection.
evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by Moriarty et al., 2020, though the manuscript appropriately notes this is RNA detection, not necessarily infectious virus. This finding has important implications for environmental contamination.

result: Estimates of R0 for SARS-CoV-2 range from 2.38 (95% CI: 2.04-2.77) to 2.9 (95% CI: 2.1-4.5) from different modeling studies.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by peer-reviewed epidemiological modeling studies (Li et al., 2020a; Park et al., 2020a). The range of estimates reflects uncertainty in early epidemic data and different modeling approaches.

result: Median estimates for latent and infectious periods are approximately 3.69 and 3.48 days, respectively.
evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by Li et al., 2020a epidemiological modeling. These parameters are critical for understanding transmission dynamics and designing interventions.

result: Median time to clinical recovery is ~2 weeks for mild cases and 3-6 weeks for severe/critical cases.
evaluation: Claims C121-C122 are supported by WHO data. These recovery timelines are important for healthcare planning and understanding disease burden.

result: Infection fatality rate (IFR) estimates range from 0.3-1.3% based on multiple approaches including repatriation data, Diamond Princess cohort, and epidemiological modeling.
evaluation: Claims C123-C128 synthesize IFR estimates from multiple peer-reviewed studies using different methodologies (Verity et al., 2020; Ferguson et al., 2020; Nishiura et al., 2020; Russell et al., 2020; Mizumoto et al., 2020). The range reflects genuine uncertainty and methodological differences. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges this is a "crude range" and notes important caveats about age-stratification and population differences.

result: SARS-CoV-2 spike protein is primed by TMPRSS2 protease.
evaluation: Claim C136 is supported by established knowledge about coronavirus entry mechanisms and is shown in Figure 1. TMPRSS2 priming is a well-documented step in SARS-CoV-2 cell entry.
